section.title: Overview
section.para: A Scaly program can be split across several source files, and it can depend on other packages. There are no build files, manifests, or configuration files — three statements inside the source itself organize everything:

listitem.para: module loads another source file into the current program or package.
package declares a dependency on another package.
use makes types defined in another module visible in the current file.

section.title: Modules
section.para: Every source file is a module. The statement module shapes loads the file shapes.scaly from the directory of the file that declares it and makes it part of the program:

A module may declare child modules of its own. Those live in a directory named after the parent module: if compiler.scaly declares module lexer, the child is loaded from compiler/lexer.scaly. This mirrors how the standard library and the compiler themselves are laid out.
Top-level statements of a loaded module are ignored — only its definitions become part of the program. Programs have top-level statements; libraries consist of definitions only.

section.title: Packages
section.para: A package is a source distribution. Its version is encoded in its filesystem path — packages/scaly/0.1.0/ — and that path is the single source of truth; there is no separate version manifest. The statement

declares a dependency on that package. A package is looked for among the packages of the installation, $SCALY_HOME/packages/ (the installed programs set SCALY_HOME themselves), and then among the project's own, ./packages/ under the directory the compiler runs in. So a project brings the packages the installation does not have by putting them beside its sources, and it cannot put a package of its own in front of an installed one of the same name. Without SCALY_HOME only the current directory is searched. A declared package that is nowhere fails the compile with an error naming the places.

The version in a declaration is a minimum. One compilation takes one version of a package, and where a program reaches the same package through several declarations — its own and those of the packages it uses — it takes the highest version any of them names: a program that asks for json 0.1.5 and uses a package that asks for json 0.1.2 is built, with 0.1.5 for both. That holds among versions that go together — within one major version, and below 1.0 within one second number ( says why); two versions that do not go together are refused, with a message naming who asked for each. Nothing else decides: there is no lock file and no solver, the versions follow from the declarations alone, and adding a dependency can raise a version but never lower one. A package's root file declares the packages it uses itself, so a program names only the packages it calls directly; circular package dependencies are forbidden.

The standard library package scaly is the implicit prelude: every program depends on it automatically, and its types are visible everywhere without any use statement. Pass --no-prelude to compile without it, for bare-metal or embedded targets. See for what the standard library provides.

section.title: Packages from a git repository
section.para: A declaration may name where its package comes from, as a string after the version:

The source is a git repository that holds the package at packages/json/0.1.3/ — the layout a project's own packages have. One repository serves every version it has published (). "github.com/someone/json" stands for https://github.com/someone/json.git; an address with a scheme, a user@host:path address and a local path are taken as they are, and whatever git needs to reach a private repository is git's business. A version is required where a source is given.

scaly run, scaly test and scaly build fetch what a program declares before they compile it, and what the fetched packages declare in their turn; scalyc never reaches the network and says which commands do. This needs git on the PATH. A fetched package is kept under ~/.scaly/packages/ (SCALY_PACKAGES names another place), by source, name and version, with its files read-only; nothing is written into the project. It is the third place a package is looked for, after the installation and the project's ./packages/ — so copying a package there is how a project keeps its own copy, and editing that copy is how it patches a dependency.

A version the package's record names is taken from the commit named there, any other from the head of the default branch. A published version does not change (). The first fetch remembers the commit and the content of the version's directory beside it; a version that is fetched again and is no longer what it was is refused, with both commits named. One package comes from one source: a program that reaches it through two different sources is refused, while two spellings of one address are one source.
A package may bring C or assembly files, which are compiled on the machine that builds it; the tool says so when it fetches one.

No name carries its package: a function that two packages each define would be one function in the linked program. The tool compares what the packages of a program define and refuses such a pair, naming both packages and the function.

section.title: Versions, and what publishing means
section.para: The rules of a package's versions are few, and the tool checks them.
A version is a directory. packages/json/0.1.3/ is version 0.1.3 of json, and the next version is another directory beside it. There are no tags, no registry and no manifest.
Published is what the package's record names. Beside its version directories a package keeps the file packages/json/published, a line for each published version:

The version, the commit its directory lay at when it was published, and the git tree of that directory. scaly publish writes the lines; nobody else needs to. A version directory without a line is a version being written: it may change from commit to commit, on the default branch too, and a program that declares it gets it as it stands — and is told when it has changed since.

A published version does not change. Its line stays as it is, and its directory, while it is in the tree, stays the tree the line names. A correction, however small, is a new version: copy the directory, change the copy.

A published version may leave the tree. The line names the commit that holds it, and a build that declares the version fetches that commit. So a repository need not carry every version it ever published side by side: the directories being worked on are in the tree, the others in its history. Removing one is an ordinary commit that deletes the directory and leaves the record alone.

The number says what changed. A new version is compared with the one before it — the highest lower version, in the tree or in the record — by what the two declare: every function, procedure, operator and initializer with its parameters and its result, every record with its fields, every union with its variants, every constant, global and alias. Bodies are not part of it, a generic routine's body neither.

row.entry: a declaration is gone or reads differently
declarations were added, none is gone

section.para: A version below 1.0 has promised nothing yet, so there a breaking change costs the second number; 1.0.0 is the statement that what the package declares is meant to stay. A build follows the same reading: the highest version asked for stands in for the lower ones where the table says nothing was taken away — within one first number from 1.0 on, within one second number below it. 0.2.0 does not stand in for 0.1.5, and a program that reaches both is told so.

The comparison is deliberately strict. Declarations are compared as they are written, comments and line breaks apart: a renamed parameter, a constant's new value, a field added to a record all count as a declaration that reads differently. And nothing in a package is private, so every declaration counts.

Both run at the root of the package's repository and speak with the remote origin (another remote, an address or a path may follow). scaly publish --check changes nothing: it says whether every published version is still what its line names, whether the remote's record is still all here, and whether every new version's number says what it changed. A version that understates its change is refused with the declarations that are gone and the number it takes at least; a new version that does not compile is refused too. It answers 0 when all is well, 1 when a rule is broken and 2 when it could not ask — no repository, or the remote out of reach. It belongs in the package's own test run, so a change to a published version is noticed before it is pushed and not by the first program that fetches it.

scaly publish checks the same and then publishes what is new: each new version gets its line — the commit is the current one, so the version must be committed —, the record is committed, and both commits are pushed. From then on the version is fixed.

Making the next version of a package is therefore: copy packages/json/0.1.3/ to the directory of the number the change takes, work and commit there as long as it takes, and scaly publish when it is done. A package that is released together with a program — a compiler with its parser, say — publishes a version with each release and works on the next one in between.

section.title: Starting a package
section.para: creates shapes/packages/shapes/0.1.0/shapes.scaly: a package with one function and its test. Its root file declares the packages it uses — the standard library too, which only a program gets without saying so:

scaly test packages/shapes/0.1.0/shapes.scaly runs its tests. A program in the directory that holds packages/ uses it with package shapes 0.1.0; once the directory is a git repository somewhere, any program does, by naming that repository as the source.

section.title: The programs of a package
section.para: A package that is a library first may still bring programs — a parser its validator and its normalizer, say. The programs a package offers are the files of the directory programs/ beside its root file, each a program named after its file:
section.programlisting: packages/shapes/0.1.0/ shapes.scaly the library shapes/ its modules programs/ shapes.scaly the program "shapes" shapes_check.scaly the program "shapes_check"
section.para: A program there is an ordinary program that declares the package it belongs to, without a source — its package and the others of the same repository lie beside it:
One of the programs may be called like the package. Other program files a package keeps — drivers for its tests, experiments — stay outside programs/ and are not offered.
section.programlisting: scaly install github.com/someone/shapes shapes 0.1.0 scaly install github.com/someone/shapes shapes 0.1.0 shapes_check
section.para: fetches the package from that repository, builds its programs — all of them, or the one named — optimised as scaly build --release does, and puts them beside scaly itself, in ~/.scaly/bin (SCALY_BIN names another place). A package without programs/ is a library, and scaly install says so.

scaly install without arguments lists what it has installed — program, package, version and source —, and scaly uninstall shapes_check removes one of those. It goes by its own record and removes nothing else of that directory.

section.title: Imports and Visibility
section.para: Type definitions are private to their module by default. A type defined in another module — even one loaded into the same program with module — is hidden until the current file imports it with a use statement. This keeps every file's dependencies explicit: the list of use statements at the top of a file is a complete inventory of the outside types the file relies on.

section.title: What Is Visible Without an Import
section.para: Three kinds of types need no use statement:

listitem.para: Types defined in the same file.
Types of the prelude — the standard library (String, Vector, Option, …) is always visible.

The namespace of a declared child module. When a file declares module geometry and geometry.scaly defines a namespace of the same name, that namespace is visible in the declaring file, so its members can be reached qualified:

section.para: Visibility applies to named type definitions. Free functions are resolved through their namespaces and are not gated separately.

section.title: Importing a Single Type
section.para: A use statement names a type by its full dotted path. The path starts with the program or package name, followed by the module path, ending in the type name:
section.programlisting: use myprog.shapes.Box ; Box from module shapes of program myprog use scalyc.compiler.Modeler ; Modeler from package scalyc
section.para: A module that is named after the single type it defines — the file Modeler.scaly defining Modeler — is addressed once, as the path spells it; the module and the type do not appear as two separate path segments.

section.title: Importing Everything from a Module
section.para: A trailing * imports every type a module defines:
section.programlisting:
module shapes use myprog.shapes.*
let b Box(3, 4) ; Box is visible through the glob if b.area() = 12 print("glob works")
section.para: Globs are convenient for a module whose types are used pervasively. Prefer single-type imports when a file uses only one or two names from a module — they document the dependency more precisely.

section.title: When a Type Is Not Visible
section.para: Referencing a type that exists in the program but has not been imported fails the compile. The error names the module that defines the type and states the exact use line that would import it:
section.programlisting: myprog.scaly:3:7: error: function not found: Box - defined in myprog.shapes but not visible here; add: use myprog.shapes.Box
section.para: Two compiler flags support working with visibility: --no-use-vis disables enforcement entirely (every type in the program is visible everywhere, the pre-visibility behavior), and --use-vis prints an advisory report of every reference that strict visibility would reject — useful when migrating an existing codebase, to collect the needed use lines before turning enforcement on.
